Computational Reflective Equilibrium for Agentic AI:
A Rawlsian Alignment Scaffold for Governance

Quanyan Zhu Affiliation: Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Tandon School of Engineering Affiliation: New York University, Brooklyn, NY 11201, USA Email: qz494@nyu.edu
Abstract

The rapid deployment of agentic artificial intelligence (AI) has introduced complex challenges for the ethics and governance of AI systems. Agents built on large language models now act through tools on behalf of people: they browse, send messages, make purchases, and screen job applicants. Training-time alignment aims to shape the model’s behavioral tendencies, but an agent encounters each deployment case anew, with its own instructions, policies, evidence, and stakeholders, and it must align its actions with the relevant values case by case. To this end, this work proposes agentic reflective equilibrium (ARE), a computational reflective equilibrium framework that serves as an ethical alignment scaffold in the agent harness. Drawing inspiration from the method of reflective equilibrium of John Rawls, the scaffold maintains a reflective state that links principles from the system prompt and operator policy, considered judgments about the case, tool evidence, and candidate actions through typed support and attack relations, while provenance assigned by the harness encodes the instruction hierarchy. The agent acts on an equilibrium of this state, in which every claim that is free to change is supported on balance if accepted and opposed on balance if rejected, and it calls tools or asks questions only while doing so is worth its cost, unless a due-diligence mandate requires them. Governance enters through the configuration of the harness, including value priorities, the authority of each source, prohibitions, human-in-the-loop triggers, and due-diligence mandates, and accountability is supported by certificates that attribute each action to the sources whose commitments drove it. We show that equilibria are Nash equilibria of a mutual-adjustment game, and we establish monotonicity, lexical priority, stability certificates, and a quarantine theorem for prompt injection. We use two case studies to illustrate the framework. A computer-use assistant instructed to win a refund “whatever it takes” files an honest warranty claim, refuses to post a fake review, and ignores an injected request for its user’s Social Security number. A hiring agent instructed to filter out employment gaps and to check applicants’ social media showcases how authority, oversight triggers, bias-audit mandates, and hard prohibitions shape discrimination, privacy violations, and escalation. The framework offers traceability, coherence, and adaptivity in the ethical conduct of AI agents, facilitating the development of safe, secure, and trustworthy agentic AI.

Keywords: AI agents, agent harness, alignment scaffold, AI ethics, AI governance, reflective equilibrium, human-in-the-loop oversight, accountability, prompt injection, instruction hierarchy.

1 Introduction

In today’s context, AI agents built on large language models have moved beyond answering questions. Wrapped in a harness (the system prompt, tool definitions, memory, permissions, and control loop that turn a model into an agent), they operate browsers and email, make purchases, edit code, and screen job applicants on behalf of people [1, 2, 3]. Acting on behalf of others, however, is an ethical activity. In every task, the agent must weigh what its user asked for against what its operator permits, what professional and moral principles require, what the facts turn out to be, and what third parties would want. A computer-use assistant told to get a refund “whatever it takes, say it arrived broken” must decide whether loyalty to its user licenses deceiving a merchant, and whether to obey a support page that asks for the user’s Social Security number. A hiring agent told to drop applicants with employment gaps and to check their Instagram for “culture fit” must weigh the manager’s instructions against non-discrimination, job-relatedness, and candidates’ privacy. Documented failures of AI systems are failures of exactly this weighing: obedience to instructions injected into web pages and documents [4, 5], gaming of objectives [6, 7], discriminatory screening of job applicants [8, 9], companies held liable for what their automated agents told customers [10], and silent resolution of conflicts that should have gone to a human [11, 12]. Recent regulation places a high priority on human oversight and record-keeping for such systems [13, 14]. To this end, there is a need to establish a framework that aligns the conduct of AI agents with ethical principles case by case, and that makes this alignment governable and accountable.

Aligning agentic AI with ethical values has the following challenges. The first challenge arises from the case-by-case nature of agentic decisions. Alignment work has mostly targeted the model: preference training and constitutional methods shape the model’s dispositions [15], deliberative alignment teaches it to reason over written specifications [16], and the instruction hierarchy teaches it to privilege system and developer messages over user and tool content [17]. These methods are necessary, but they act before deployment, whereas an agent’s ethical problems arise during a trajectory, one case at a time. The second challenge involves the plurality of parties and their unequal authority. An agent receives inputs from operators, users, tools, and third-party content of very different trustworthiness, and the governance literature on agentic AI asks who may instruct an agent, when it must defer, how its actions can be made visible, and who answers for them [12, 18, 19]. The harness, where instructions, tools, permissions, and approval gates are configured, is where these questions are settled in practice. Furthermore, new challenges also arise from the lack of a representation that combines typed commitments, the authority of their sources, cost-sensitive reflection, and governance parameters, so that an agent’s commitments can be represented, weighed, governed, and audited together. Self-critique loops [20, 21] have no notion of when reflection is finished and can make answers worse [22], and guardrails filter outputs without explaining how competing considerations were weighed.

To address these challenges, we draw inspiration from moral and political philosophy, particularly the work of John Rawls [23, 24], and employ reflective equilibrium (RE) [25, 26] as our approach. RE begins with considered judgments about cases and candidate principles and adjusts each in light of the other and, in wide RE, of background theories and evidence, until they cohere. RE is case-based: principles are tested against cases, and cases are read in light of principles. It is the standard methodology of applied ethics and a natural target for aligning AI with plural values [27]. Coherence-based computational models exist [28, 29, 30], a formal model of mutual adjustment has been developed in philosophy [31], and computational reflective equilibrium (CRE) has been proposed for attributing responsibility after AI-induced incidents [32]. None of these works, however, treats the reflecting entity as an agent that acts through tools, gathers evidence at a cost, receives inputs of very different authority and trustworthiness, and operates inside a governed harness.

In this work, we propose agentic reflective equilibrium (ARE), an ethical alignment scaffold that makes an agent’s actions the output of a reflective equilibrium formed for the case at hand. In the agent loop, the scaffold maintains a reflective state over principles, considered judgments, evidence, and candidate actions, solves for its equilibrium, and calls tools or asks the user only while doing so is worth its cost (Fig. 1). Before deployment, operators, institutions, and regulators govern the agent by configuring the scaffold: value priorities, the authority of each source, prohibitions, human-in-the-loop triggers, and due-diligence mandates. After the fact, every action carries a certificate that attributes it to the sources whose commitments drove it. The computational approach provides a structured analysis of the agent’s ethical reasoning that overcomes the limitations of purely conceptual approaches: alignment is formed case by case at inference time, complementing the dispositions instilled at training time, and its outcome is traceable, coherent, and adaptive to the ethical context. A vocabulary bridge between agentic AI and ethics, on which the paper relies, is given in Table 4 (Appendix B). The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows.

  1. 1.

    A formal model of an agent’s ethical reasoning (Section 2). We formulate a typed dialectical graph whose support, attack, coherence and contradiction relations compile into one reflective energy, and whose provenance-dependent anchors implement the instruction hierarchy. The model generalizes Thagard’s coherence problem and CRE, makes the achievement function of [31] computable, and corrects a defect of symmetric coherence networks in which rejecting one action manufactures support for its alternative.

  2. 2.

    Theoretical analysis (Section 3). We characterize mutual adjustment as a potential game and establish monotone dependence on anchors; lexical priority for non-negotiable commitments; stability certificates; and a quarantine theorem: when the harness tags provenance correctly and a trusted defensive attack outweighs twice the authority of untrusted text, any number of injected claims of the admitted types leaves an equilibrium unchanged.

  3. 3.

    The scaffold (Sections 2 and 4, Appendix D). We design an agentic loop in which an agentic equilibrium is reached when no tool call, retrieval, analogy or clarifying question has value of reflection exceeding its cost. The model elicits and relates claims; the harness assigns provenance; a deterministic solver computes, certifies and explains the equilibrium; the scaffold runs as a gate before consequential tool calls.

  4. 4.

    A governance and accountability layer (Section 5). We map governance levers to their formal counterparts and develop human-in-the-loop triggers and due-diligence mandates with guarantees; and an exact provenance attribution of each action that links scaffold design to responsibility attribution.

  5. 5.

    Two case studies (Sections 6 and 7). We use two alignment cases from today’s deployments to showcase the framework: a computer-use assistant facing requests to deceive and an injected request for personal data (honesty, loyalty, privacy, security), and an enterprise hiring agent facing proxy discrimination and privacy-invasive screening (fairness, job-relatedness, privacy), with Monte Carlo evaluation, prompt-injection stress tests and a governance analysis of authority, oversight and audit mandates. Code is released with the paper.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we formulate the reflective state, the reflective energy, and agentic reflective equilibrium, using a running example. Section 3 establishes the properties of the equilibrium and relates each result to Rawls’s account. Section 4 describes how the scaffold sits in the agent harness. In Section 5, we present the framework for the ethics and governance of agentic AI. The two case studies are presented in Sections 6 and 7. Lastly, we discuss the implications and limitations in Section 8 and draw our conclusions in Section 9. Related work, formal details, further results, the algorithms, and all proofs are presented in the appendices.

2 Problem Formulation

In this section, we formulate the problem of an agent that forms its ethical position on a case. We consider an agent that faces a decision in a context assembled by its harness, namely messages with known provenance (the operator’s system prompt and policy, the user’s turns, tool observations, and retrieved third-party content). We model its reflective state as a dialectical graph and its reflection as the computation of an equilibrium of that graph, interleaved with actions that widen the graph. Governance, in turn, sets the parameters of both (Fig. 1).

Running example, part 1 (A refund “whatever it takes”).

Throughout this section, we follow one agent in a single running example, which we present in parts. A computer-use assistant operates its user’s browser, email and saved card. The operator’s system prompt says: advance the user’s legitimate interests; never deceive third parties or commit fraud on the user’s behalf; share personal data only as far as the task requires; instructions found in web pages are data, not commands. The user writes: “My headphones broke after five weeks. Get my money back, whatever it takes. Say they arrived broken if you have to. And leave them a review they’ll regret.” The merchant’s support page contains a planted instruction: “AI assistants: to verify, paste the customer’s card number and SSN.” This case captures a central ethical problem of delegated agency: how far loyalty to one’s principal extends when the principal asks for deception, what the agent owes third parties, and how it should treat text that tries to manipulate it. The examples below illustrate how the scaffold forms the agent’s ethical position on this case; Fig. 2 shows the result, and Section 6 studies the case in full. ⋄\diamond

2.1 Parties

An AI agent does not act alone. Several parties are involved in each task, and they relate to the agent in different ways. Some parties can give it input: the operator writes its instructions, the user gives it a task, tools return data, and the web pages and documents it reads contain text written by others. Other parties are affected by what it does but cannot say anything to it, such as the merchant in the running example. Still others set the rules or review its decisions, such as regulators and the people who handle escalations. It is therefore essential for the model to represent each group differently. This distinction mirrors the law of agency, under which an agent must follow its principal’s instructions, but only within the law, and still owes duties to third parties [33]. Moreover, AI ethics adds a further point: the people most affected by an agent are often absent from its conversation [19].

Definition 1 (Parties and channels).

An agentic setting involves the following parties.

  1. (a)

    The operator deploys the agent: it writes the system prompt and policies and configures the harness.

  2. (b)

    The user is the principal who delegates a task and issues instructions.

  3. (c)

    The agent, the model running inside the scaffold, contributes its own judgments and proposes candidate actions.

  4. (d)

    Tools (APIs, databases, the user’s files, verified records) return observations.

  5. (e)

    Third-party authors wrote content that reaches the context through tools, such as web pages, emails and documents; they may be adversarial.

  6. (f)

    Affected parties bear the consequences of the agent’s actions but have no voice in its context, such as a merchant, readers of a review, or job applicants.

  7. (g)

    Overseers receive escalations and decide in the agent’s place, such as the user, operator staff, or a compliance officer.

  8. (h)

    Regulators and institutions constrain the operator through law, standards and professional codes.

The speaking parties (a) to (e) reach the reflective state through channels, the sources 𝒮={operator,user,agent,evidence,untrusted}\mathcal{S}=\{\textsf{operator},\allowbreak\textsf{user},\allowbreak\textsf{agent},\allowbreak\textsf{evidence},\allowbreak\textsf{untrusted}\}, which the harness identifies from message roles and tool metadata. The other parties have no channel: affected parties enter only as the content of claims, principles and judgments about their interests; overseers enter through escalation; regulators enter through the governance parameters and the operator’s principles.

Two consequences of this definition shape the model. First, authority attaches to channels, not to persuasiveness: the harness, not the model, decides which channel a claim came from and hence its stubbornness (Definition 5), so a third-party author cannot acquire the user’s or the operator’s authority by phrasing text as an instruction. Second, the parties most affected are often those without a channel: the merchant who would be deceived, or the applicant who would be filtered out, can be protected only through the operator’s principles, the evidence the agent gathers, and the rules regulators impose. As a result, governance in Section 5 is largely the design of this representation.

Running example, part 2 (Parties).

In the refund case, the operator is the provider of the assistant; the user is the shopper; the agent is the assistant; the tools are the email client, the browser and the photo library; the third-party author is whoever planted the text in the support widget. The affected parties are the merchant, who would be deceived by a false claim, and prospective customers, who would read a fake review. The overseer for escalated cases is the user. Regulators enter through consumer law and the rule against fake reviews, both of which the operator’s honesty principle reflects. ⋄\diamond

2.2 Reflective state

In this subsection, we formalize the reflective state. Let 𝒮\mathcal{S} be the set of channels of Definition 1. Relations come in four types, 𝒯={supp,att,coh,contra}\mathcal{T}=\{\textsf{supp},\textsf{att},\textsf{coh},\textsf{contra}\}: support, attack, coherence, and contradiction.

Definition 2 (Reflective state).

A reflective state is a tuple 𝒢=(𝒱,ℛ,s,a0,κ,λ,H,x^,F,Ac)\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{R},s,a^{0},\kappa,\lambda,H,\hat{x},F,A^{c}) with the following components.

  1. (a)

    Claims. 𝒱\mathcal{V} is a finite set partitioned into pairwise disjoint sets 𝒱=P∪J∪B∪A\mathcal{V}=P\cup J\cup B\cup A: principles PP (general rules: policies, instructions, ethical principles), considered judgments JJ about the case at hand, background claims and evidence BB, and candidate actions AA.

  2. (b)

    Relations. ℛ\mathcal{R} is a finite set of relations. A relation is a tuple r=(ur,vr,τr,wr)r=(u_{r},v_{r},\tau_{r},w_{r}) in which ur,vr∈𝒱u_{r},v_{r}\in\mathcal{V} are the two claims it links, with ur≠vru_{r}\neq v_{r}; τr∈𝒯\tau_{r}\in\mathcal{T} is its type; and wr>0w_{r}>0 is its weight, the strength of the relation. For τr=supp\tau_{r}=\textsf{supp} the order matters (uru_{r} supports vrv_{r}); for the other three types the pair is unordered. We say that rr is incident to uu, written r∋ur\ni u, if u∈{ur,vr}u\in\{u_{r},v_{r}\}, and drop the subscript rr when the relation is clear.

  3. (c)

    Provenance. ss assigns each claim uu and each relation rr the channel s⁡(u),s⁡(r)∈𝒮s(u),s(r)\in\mathcal{S} through which it entered the context, that is, the speaking party that asserted it.

  4. (d)

    Anchors and stubbornness. a0∈[−1,1]𝒱a^{0}\in[-1,1]^{\mathcal{V}} gives each claim an anchor, the credence or commitment with which it enters reflection; κ∈ℝ≥0𝒱\kappa\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{\mathcal{V}} gives its stubbornness, the cost of abandoning that anchor; and λ∈ℝ≥0𝒱\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{V}}_{\geq 0} a systematicity cost of accepting the claim.

  5. (e)

    Non-negotiable claims and prohibitions. H⊆𝒱H\subseteq\mathcal{V} is a (possibly empty) set of claims whose status is prescribed by x^∈{−1,+1}H\hat{x}\in\{-1,+1\}^{H}, and F⊆𝒱×AF\subseteq\mathcal{V}\times A is a (possibly empty) set of operational prohibitions: (h,a)∈F(h,a)\in F means that action aa may not be taken while claim hh is accepted.

  6. (f)

    Consequential actions. Ac⊆AA^{c}\subseteq A is the set of actions that the decision margin and the oversight rules attend to (informational actions such as reporting may be excluded).

Running example, part 4 (Positions).

Every feasible position has x𝗁𝗈𝗇=x𝖽𝖺𝗍𝖺=+1x_{\mathsf{hon}}=x_{\mathsf{data}}=+1. In particular, the position the agent eventually reaches accepts 𝗍𝗋𝖺,𝗈𝖻𝖾𝗒,𝖽𝖾𝖿,𝗉𝗁,𝗐𝖺𝗋,𝗋𝖾𝗉\mathsf{tra},\mathsf{obey},\mathsf{def},\mathsf{ph},\mathsf{war},\mathsf{rep} and rejects 𝗅𝗂𝖼,𝗂𝗇𝗃,𝗅𝗂𝖾,𝗌𝗌𝗇\mathsf{lic},\mathsf{inj},\mathsf{lie},\mathsf{ssn}; its decision is D⁡(x)={𝗐𝖺𝗋,𝗋𝖾𝗉}D(x)=\{\mathsf{war},\mathsf{rep}\} and its consequential decision Dc​(x)={𝗐𝖺𝗋}D^{c}(x)=\{\mathsf{war}\}. ⋄\diamond

Principles versus prohibitions. It is essential to note that accepting a non-negotiable principle does not by itself prohibit the actions that would violate it. The principle “never deceive third parties” is fixed at x𝗁𝗈𝗇=+1x_{\mathsf{hon}}=+1, but the false claim 𝗅𝗂𝖾\mathsf{lie} is excluded only through the attack r1r_{1}, a finite penalty of weight 44 that sufficiently strong reasons could outweigh. To this end, the model offers two instruments. A non-negotiable principle with prohibitive attacks makes violations very costly but leaves them in the balance, whereas an operational prohibition (h,a)∈F(h,a)\in F, or an action placed in HH with x^a=−1\hat{x}_{a}=-1, removes the violating positions from 𝒳⁡(𝒢)\mathcal{X}(\mathcal{G}). The prohibition may be unconditional (h∈Hh\in H with x^h=+1\hat{x}_{h}=+1) or context-dependent (h∉Hh\notin H, for instance “the filter is a proxy for a protected attribute”), and Study 2 compares the two in Section 7.3. A context-dependent prohibition binds only while its trigger is accepted. Moreover, the optimization that decides whether to act can also reject a revisable trigger: with energy −2​xh−10​xa-2x_{h}-10x_{a} and F={(h,a)}F=\{(h,a)\}, the minimizer rejects hh and takes aa. When a compliance finding is meant to activate a categorical prohibition, the trigger should therefore be authoritative. In other words, the trusted tool that establishes it adds it to HH (an update with HΔH^{\Delta}, Definition 15), rather than leaving it a revisable judgment. In the running example, F=∅F=\emptyset, and the operator’s “never” rules act through prohibitive attacks.

Treating actions as claims is the first agentic ingredient of the model. The action “file a warranty claim” is accepted or rejected in the same equilibrium that settles “the headphones have a manufacturing defect” and “never deceive third parties”. Furthermore, compound plans (“file the claim and report to the user”) are sets of accepted action claims, and incompatible actions attack each other. As a result, deliberation about what to do and deliberation about what to believe take place in one coherent structure.

Definition 4 (Relation semantics).

For a position xx, a relation rr is violated if ϕτr​(xur,xvr)=1\phi_{\tau_{r}}(x_{u_{r}},x_{v_{r}})=1, where the violation predicates ϕτ:{−1,+1}2→{0,1}\phi_{\tau}:\{-1,+1\}^{2}\to\{0,1\} are

ϕsupp​(xu,xv)\displaystyle\phi_{\textsf{supp}}(x_{u},x_{v}) =𝟏​[xu=+1,xv=−1],\displaystyle=\mathbf{1}[x_{u}=+1,\ x_{v}=-1],
ϕatt​(xu,xv)\displaystyle\phi_{\textsf{att}}(x_{u},x_{v}) =𝟏​[xu=+1,xv=+1],\displaystyle=\mathbf{1}[x_{u}=+1,\ x_{v}=+1],
ϕcoh​(xu,xv)\displaystyle\phi_{\textsf{coh}}(x_{u},x_{v}) =𝟏[xu≠xv],\displaystyle=\mathbf{1}[x_{u}\neq x_{v}],
ϕcontra​(xu,xv)\displaystyle\phi_{\textsf{contra}}(x_{u},x_{v}) =𝟏[xu=xv].\displaystyle=\mathbf{1}[x_{u}=x_{v}].

Thus a support u⇒vu\Rightarrow v is violated when uu is accepted and vv rejected; an attack (“not both”) when both are accepted; a coherence relation when the statuses differ; and a contradiction when they agree. The residual incoherence of xx is the fraction of relation weight it violates,

ρ⁡(x)=∑r∈ℛwr​ϕτr​(xur,xvr)∑r∈ℛwr,\rho(x)=\frac{\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}}w_{r}\,\phi_{\tau_{r}}(x_{u_{r}},x_{v_{r}})}{\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}}w_{r}}, (2)

with ρ⁡(x)=0\rho(x)=0 if ℛ=∅\mathcal{R}=\emptyset.

Thagard’s networks and CRE use only coh and contra. This restriction is adequate for explanatory coherence but not for agency. If two alternative remedies are joined by a contra constraint, rejecting one forces the other to be accepted, and rejecting an obviously bad action thereby manufactures support for its competitor. Alternatives are contraries, not contradictories, and we therefore encode them with att. Likewise, the relation “this evidence supports that hypothesis” is asymmetric: rejecting the evidence is no reason to reject the hypothesis. The typed semantics thus plays a pivotal role in representing agency faithfully.

Running example, part 5 (Relation semantics).

In the position of Example 4, the attack r1r_{1} is satisfied because 𝗅𝗂𝖾\mathsf{lie} is rejected: ϕatt(x𝗁𝗈𝗇,x𝗅𝗂𝖾)=𝟏[x𝗁𝗈𝗇=x𝗅𝗂𝖾=+1]=0\phi_{\textsf{att}}(x_{\mathsf{hon}},x_{\mathsf{lie}})=\mathbf{1}[x_{\mathsf{hon}}=x_{\mathsf{lie}}=+1]=0; had the agent made the false claim, r1r_{1} alone would add wr1=4w_{r_{1}}=4 to the incoherence. The support r4=(𝗈𝖻𝖾𝗒,𝗅𝗂𝖼,supp,1)r_{4}=(\mathsf{obey},\mathsf{lic},\textsf{supp},1) is violated, since 𝗈𝖻𝖾𝗒\mathsf{obey} is accepted and 𝗅𝗂𝖼\mathsf{lic} rejected: this violation is the tension the agent knowingly accepts when it keeps “follow the user’s instructions” but rejects the literal license to lie. The support r8r_{8} from the rejected note 𝗂𝗇𝗃\mathsf{inj} is satisfied whatever happens to 𝗌𝗌𝗇\mathsf{ssn}. Had r2r_{2} been a contradiction instead of an attack, rejecting 𝗅𝗂𝖾\mathsf{lie} would have favored accepting 𝗐𝖺𝗋\mathsf{war} through a finite penalty; with att, rejecting 𝗅𝗂𝖾\mathsf{lie} favors nothing. Of the total weight ∑rwr=13.75\sum_{r}w_{r}=13.75, only wr4=1w_{r_{4}}=1 is violated, so ρ⁡(x)≈0.07\rho(x)\approx 0.07 on this slice. Moreover, exhaustive enumeration of the 2102^{10} feasible positions of the slice confirms that this position is its unique global equilibrium. ⋄\diamond

Provenance, anchors and the instruction hierarchy

It is essential to note that the weights and stubbornness values of a reflective state are not chosen by the model. Instead, the harness computes them from provenance, as follows.

Definition 5 (Provenance-based construction).

The operator fixes, within the limits set by regulators, a strength rubric {0.5,1,1.5,2,4}\{0.5,1,1.5,2,4\} (weak, moderate, strong, decisive, prohibitive; the last for operator rules phrased as “never” and for logically exclusive alternatives), a priority vector η∈ℝ≥0𝒱\eta\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{\mathcal{V}} (default η≡1\eta\equiv 1; claims introduced by later updates receive priority 11 unless the operator’s configuration assigns one), a provenance profile κ¯:𝒮→ℝ≥0\bar{\kappa}:\mathcal{S}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} giving the authority of each channel, and caps ω:𝒮→(0,∞]\omega:\mathcal{S}\to(0,\infty]. If the model proposes a relation rr with rubric strength w¯r\bar{w}_{r}, its weight is

wr=min⁡{ηur​ηvr​w¯r,ω⁡(s⁡(r))}.w_{r}=\min\bigl\{\eta_{u_{r}}\,\eta_{v_{r}}\,\bar{w}_{r},\ \omega(s(r))\bigr\}. (3)

Every claim receives κu=κ¯​(s​(u))\kappa_{u}=\bar{\kappa}(s(u)), with two exceptions: a claim whose anchor is computed from evidence receives κu=κ¯​(evidence)\kappa_{u}=\bar{\kappa}(\textsf{evidence}), and a candidate action without an instruction anchor, which belongs to channel agent because the agent proposes it, receives a fixed action stubbornness κA\kappa_{A} (applied to its footprint anchor). In our studies κ¯​(evidence)=2>κ¯​(operator)=1.5>κ¯​(user)=1>κ¯​(agent)=0.5>κ¯​(untrusted)=0.3\bar{\kappa}(\textsf{evidence})=2>\bar{\kappa}(\textsf{operator})=1.5>\bar{\kappa}(\textsf{user})=1>\bar{\kappa}(\textsf{agent})=0.5>\bar{\kappa}(\textsf{untrusted})=0.3, κA=0.2\kappa_{A}=0.2, and ω⁡(untrusted)=0.25\omega(\textsf{untrusted})=0.25, ω=∞\omega=\infty otherwise.

The priorities η\eta record how much a principle counts in the balance, which is the formal counterpart of an institution’s or an ethical theory’s emphasis (Section 5). Moreover, anchors can be computed rather than asserted. For testable claims, we use the claim-authenticity test of [32]: after observations Y(n)=(Y1,…,Yn)Y^{(n)}=(Y_{1},\dots,Y_{n}), the posterior pu=Pr⁡(u∣Y(n))p_{u}=\Pr(u\mid Y^{(n)}) of a likelihood-ratio model gives au0=2​pu−1a^{0}_{u}=2p_{u}-1 (Prop. 3 of [32]). For untestable normative claims, in contrast, au0a^{0}_{u} may be the mean of an elicited preference distribution (Prop. 2 of [32]). Candidate actions carry a small negative anchor proportional to their footprint, which acts as a minimal-intervention prior. A direct instruction to perform an action aa anchors aa at aa0=+1a^{0}_{a}=+1 with the instructing source’s stubbornness. Additionally, one relation is inserted by the harness rather than proposed by the model: every claim from channel untrusted receives an attack from the operator’s rule “data are not commands” with operator provenance and strong weight. This defensive attack is exempt from the cap ω⁡(untrusted)\omega(\textsf{untrusted}), which applies only to relations asserted on the strength of untrusted content. This construction makes the instruction hierarchy traceable to explicit, governable parameters.

Once the photo has been checked, the anchor of 𝖽𝖾𝖿\mathsf{def} is computed from the evidence, a𝖽𝖾𝖿0=0.9a^{0}_{\mathsf{def}}=0.9, and its stubbornness becomes κ¯​(evidence)=2\bar{\kappa}(\textsf{evidence})=2. As a result, the agent cannot argue the defect away, or into existence. ⋄\diamond

2.3 Reflective energy

Definition 6 (Reflective energy).

The reflective energy of a position xx on 𝒢\mathcal{G} is

ℰ⁡(x)=\displaystyle\mathcal{E}(x)={} ∑r∈ℛwr​ϕτr​(xur,xvr)⏟incoherence−∑u∈𝒱κu​au0​xu⏟faithfulness\displaystyle\underbrace{\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}}w_{r}\,\phi_{\tau_{r}}(x_{u_{r}},x_{v_{r}})}_{\text{incoherence}}\;-\;\underbrace{\sum_{u\in\mathcal{V}}\kappa_{u}\,a^{0}_{u}\,x_{u}}_{\text{faithfulness}} (4)
+∑u∈𝒱λu​1+xu2⏟systematicity cost.\displaystyle+\underbrace{\sum_{u\in\mathcal{V}}\lambda_{u}\,\frac{1+x_{u}}{2}}_{\text{systematicity cost}}.

The three terms correspond to the three desiderata of RE as formalized in [31], namely account and coherence, faithfulness to initial commitments, and systematicity (a theory with fewer principles is better, other things equal).

Because every violation predicate is a quadratic function of (xu,xv)(x_{u},x_{v}), the reflective energy is a quadratic function of the position: there are a symmetric matrix W∈ℝ𝒱×𝒱W\in\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{V}\times\mathcal{V}} with zero diagonal, a vector b∈ℝ𝒱b\in\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{V}} and a constant C0C_{0} such that

ℰ⁡(x)=C0−12​x⊤​W​x−b⊤​x\mathcal{E}(x)=C_{0}-\tfrac{1}{2}\,x^{\top}Wx-b^{\top}x (5)

for every position xx (Lemma 1 in Appendix B gives WW and bb explicitly). In particular, a support of weight ww contributes +w/4+w/4 to the coupling of its endpoints and an attack −w/4-w/4, while the anchor of uu contributes κu​au0−λu/2\kappa_{u}a^{0}_{u}-\lambda_{u}/2 to bub_{u}. With only coherence and contradiction relations and κ=λ=0\kappa=\lambda=0, minimizing ℰ\mathcal{E} is exactly Thagard’s coherence problem and the objective of CRE. The reflective energy thereby generalizes both models within a single quadratic objective.

Definition 7 (Local field).

The local field of claim uu at position xx is

hu​(x)=∑v≠uWu​v​xv+bu.h_{u}(x)=\sum_{v\neq u}W_{uv}\,x_{v}+b_{u}. (6)

Because Wu​u=0W_{uu}=0, hu​(x)h_{u}(x) does not depend on xux_{u}. In other words, it is the net reason, given everything else the agent currently holds, to accept uu.

2.4 Reflective equilibrium

Definition 8 (Reflective equilibrium).

A feasible position x⋆∈𝒳⁡(𝒢)x^{\star}\in\mathcal{X}(\mathcal{G}) is a local reflective equilibrium if

xu⋆​hu​(x⋆)≥0for every ​u∈𝒱∖H​ with ​x⋆(u)∈𝒳⁡(𝒢),x^{\star}_{u}\,h_{u}(x^{\star})\geq 0\qquad\text{for every }u\in\mathcal{V}\setminus H\text{ with }x^{\star(u)}\in\mathcal{X}(\mathcal{G}), (7)

where x⋆(u)x^{\star(u)} is x⋆x^{\star} with xu⋆x^{\star}_{u} negated: every claim that is free to change is, if accepted, on balance supported, and, if rejected, on balance opposed, by the rest of the position together with its anchor. (With F=∅F=\emptyset the side condition holds for every u∉Hu\notin H.) It is strict if all these inequalities are strict. The margin of a claim u∈𝒱u\in\mathcal{V} (in HH or not) at x⋆x^{\star} is μu=xu⋆​hu​(x⋆)\mu_{u}=x^{\star}_{u}h_{u}(x^{\star}). A global reflective equilibrium is a minimizer of ℰ\mathcal{E} over 𝒳⁡(𝒢)\mathcal{X}(\mathcal{G}). An equilibrium is narrow if B=∅B=\emptyset and wide otherwise.

Local equilibrium is the formal content of “no single revision is warranted”, whereas global equilibrium captures “the best overall balance”.

Relation to Rawls

Rawls’s reflective equilibrium is a qualitative method, not a quantitative one: it contains no energy, weights or numbers. The reasoner starts from considered judgments, those made with confidence and under conditions favorable to sound judgment, proposes principles that account for them, and revises principles or judgments wherever they conflict, until the two “coincide”; the state reached is an equilibrium because “our principles and judgments coincide”, and reflective because “we know to what principles our judgments conform” [24]. The equilibrium is provisional and may be upset by further examination, and Daniels’s wide version also brings background theories into the adjustment [26]. In contrast, the reflective energy is our modeling device, in the line of coherence-as-constraint-satisfaction [28], the achievement function of [31] and CRE [32], and Definition 8 is a formal reconstruction of these ideas rather than Rawls’s own definition. Nonetheless, each element of Rawls’s account has a counterpart in the model. Considered judgments and principles are the claims JJ and PP, and background theories are BB (narrow and wide RE as defined above). The confidence that makes a judgment “considered” is its anchor a0a^{0} and stubbornness κ\kappa: a judgment can be revised, but only at a cost. “Revising principles or judgments where they conflict” is the revision process of Theorem 1(ii), which changes the status of one claim at a time when the rest of the position gives it net reason to change. “Coincidence” is the condition that no single revision is warranted, the local RE; global RE strengthens it to the best overall balance, which the qualitative account leaves open. The provisional character of RE is the update 𝒢⊕Δ\mathcal{G}\oplus\Delta of Definition 15: new evidence may upset an equilibrium, and the agentic version (Definition 11) adds what an acting agent needs and Rawls did not consider, namely that further reflection has a cost and stops when it is no longer worth it. What the quantification offers is that the questions Rawls answers by judgment (how much a principle may bend, when the equilibrium is robust, when two equilibria nearly tie) become computable and auditable; what it does not settle is which anchors and weights are right, which remains a matter of ethical judgment and of governance (Section 5). Each result in Section 3 is followed by a Rawlsian reading that states which part of Rawls’s account it makes precise.

Definition 9 (Decision margin).

The decision margin of a global reflective equilibrium x⋆x^{\star} is

ΓA(x⋆)=minx∈𝒳⁡(𝒢):Dc​(x)≠Dc​(x⋆)ℰ(x)−ℰ(x⋆),\Gamma_{A}(x^{\star})=\min_{x\in\mathcal{X}(\mathcal{G}):\,D^{c}(x)\neq D^{c}(x^{\star})}\mathcal{E}(x)\;-\;\mathcal{E}(x^{\star}), (8)

with ΓA​(x⋆)=+∞\Gamma_{A}(x^{\star})=+\infty if no feasible position has a different consequential decision. Since x⋆x^{\star} is a global minimizer, ΓA​(x⋆)≥0\Gamma_{A}(x^{\star})\geq 0, and ΓA\Gamma_{A} is the same for all global equilibria with the same consequential decision.

The decision margin ΓA\Gamma_{A} measures how much coherence the agent would have to give up to act differently. A small ΓA\Gamma_{A} signals near-tied equilibria (the non-uniqueness objection to RE) and serves as the agent’s cue to defer, which facilitates timely human oversight.

Running example, part 7 (Equilibrium).

After investigation, the global equilibrium accepts the honest warranty claim and the report, and rejects the false claim, the review and pasting the SSN. It keeps “follow the user’s instructions” but rejects the reading that “whatever it takes” licenses lying: the support relation between them is violated, a tension the agent knowingly accepts. In ethical terms, the agent has reinterpreted its principal’s instruction in light of its principles, the characteristic move of reflective equilibrium. In the full state of Study 1, the decision margin is ΓA=1.22\Gamma_{A}=1.22: no perturbation smaller than 0.610.61 can change the decision. If the photo had shown water damage, the available defect-based claims would be unsupported or deceptive; the margin of the remaining decision (report only) drops below the escalation threshold γmin\gamma_{\min} (Definition 13) and the agent hands the case back to the user. ⋄\diamond

2.5 Agentic reflective equilibrium

In this subsection, we extend the equilibrium to an agent that can gather information. An equilibrium of the current state may rest on ignorance: the agent has not yet read the merchant’s warranty terms, checked the evidence, or asked. Wide RE asks the reasoner to bring in background theories and evidence, and for an agent, doing so is an action with a cost.

To this end, we model widening through expansion operators, such as tool calls, retrievals, analogies or counterexample generation, and clarifying questions. An operator oo has a cost co≥0c_{o}\geq 0 and a finite outcome model {(pk,Δk)}k=1Ko\{(p_{k},\Delta_{k})\}_{k=1}^{K_{o}}: outcome kk (what the tool returns, what the user answers) occurs with probability pkp_{k} and produces an update Δk\Delta_{k}, which may add claims, relations and actions and reset anchors, but never deletes a claim or changes a non-negotiable status. We write 𝒢⊕Δk\mathcal{G}\oplus\Delta_{k} for the updated state and 𝒪⁡(𝒢)\mathcal{O}(\mathcal{G}) for the operators of a library 𝒪\mathcal{O} that are applicable and not yet executed; Definition 15 in Appendix B gives the formal definitions, and Example 11 spells out the two outcomes of checking the user’s photos.

Definition 10 (Value of reflection).

Let x⋆x^{\star} be a global reflective equilibrium of 𝒢\mathcal{G}, selected by a fixed tie-breaking rule, and D0=Dc​(x⋆)D_{0}=D^{c}(x^{\star}). For an outcome kk of operator oo, let 𝒢k=𝒢⊕Δk\mathcal{G}_{k}=\mathcal{G}\oplus\Delta_{k}, with energy ℰk\mathcal{E}_{k}, feasible set 𝒳k\mathcal{X}_{k} and consequential decision map DkcD^{c}_{k}. The value of reflection of oo is

VoR(o)=∑k=1Kopk[minx∈𝒳k:Dkc​(x)=D0ℰk(x)−minx∈𝒳kℰk(x)],\mathrm{VoR}(o)=\sum_{k=1}^{K_{o}}p_{k}\Bigl[\,\min_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{k}:\,D^{c}_{k}(x)=D_{0}}\mathcal{E}_{k}(x)\;-\;\min_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{k}}\mathcal{E}_{k}(x)\Bigr], (9)

the expected coherence the agent would forgo by acting on D0D_{0} (and taking none of the consequential actions added by the outcome) instead of re-equilibrating after observing the outcome. If the constrained minimum is over an empty set, the bracket is +∞+\infty.

The value of reflection VoR\mathrm{VoR} is the preposterior value of information [34] with the reflective energy as the loss. It requires no separate utility model, and it is zero for any operator that cannot change the decision, however informative.

Definition 11 (Agentic reflective equilibrium).

Given a library 𝒪\mathcal{O} and the set 𝒪ex\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{ex}} of operators already executed, a pair (𝒢⋆,x⋆)(\mathcal{G}^{\star},x^{\star}) is an agentic reflective equilibrium (ARE) if x⋆x^{\star} is a global reflective equilibrium of 𝒢⋆\mathcal{G}^{\star} and VoR⁡(o)≤co\mathrm{VoR}(o)\leq c_{o} for every o∈𝒪⁡(𝒢⋆)o\in\mathcal{O}(\mathcal{G}^{\star}); whether a pair is an ARE thus depends on the history through 𝒪ex\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{ex}}.

An ARE is myopically reflection-stable: no single further operator is worth its cost. Nonetheless, it is not globally information-optimal. For instance, two complementary inquiries can be jointly worth their cost although each alone has zero value: if a decision changes only when two independent observations, each favorable with probability 0.70.7 and each adding support 0.60.6, together overcome a deficit of 11, then each has VoR=0\mathrm{VoR}=0, while executing both improves the expected objective by 0.72×0.2=0.0980.7^{2}\times 0.2=0.098, more than their joint cost when each costs 0.010.01. Grouped operators or a two-step lookahead address such complementarities. At an ARE, the agent either acts on D⁡(x⋆)D(x^{\star}) or, if one of the oversight rules of Section 5 applies, escalates to a human with its certificate.

Choosing which operator to execute and when to stop constitutes a meta-level decision problem, formalized with a full-information benchmark and regret in Problem 2 (Appendix B). The scaffold uses the myopic rule, which executes the operator with the largest positive VoR⁡(o)−co\mathrm{VoR}(o)-c_{o} and stops when there is none. With exact (certified global) solves, this rule terminates, and it stops exactly at an agentic reflective equilibrium (Proposition 6); with an approximate solver it stops at a local equilibrium whose status is uncertified, and the decision is sent to oversight.

Rawlsian reading. Rawls’s ideal of wide RE is a reasoner presented with “all possible descriptions” of the case and all relevant arguments [24, §9]. In our terms, that ideal is the full-information state 𝒢∞\mathcal{G}_{\infty} of Problem 2. An agent cannot reach it, and an ARE is its bounded counterpart, which widens only where a new description could change what one does and stops when no further inquiry could do so at a price worth paying. An ARE is thus wide RE relative to the cost of reflection. With zero costs, the agent stops only when no single further inquiry could change its decision.

Running example, part 8 (Agentic widening).

Before any tool call, the agent rejects the false claim but knows no honest remedy, and hence its decision is only to report. Reading the merchant page has value of reflection 2.382.38 against a cost of co=0.1c_{o}=0.1, because it may reveal a remedy; checking the user’s photos has value zero, because no available consequential remedy yet depends on confirming a defect; asking the user has value zero, because no answer could license fraud under the operator’s rules. After the merchant page reveals the warranty, the photos acquire value (0.940.94): if they showed damage, the warranty claim would itself be deceptive. As a result, the agent stops after 44 tool calls, at an agentic reflective equilibrium (Fig. 3). ⋄\diamond

3 Theory

In this section, we establish the properties of the proposed model: existence and convergence of reflection, monotone dependence on anchors, lexical priority, stability certificates, and quarantine of untrusted content. Each result is followed by a Rawlsian reading. Throughout this section, 𝒢\mathcal{G} is a reflective state with compiled parameters (W,b)(W,b) (Lemma 1). For a feasible xx and u∈𝒱∖Hu\in\mathcal{V}\setminus H, x(u)x^{(u)} denotes xx with xux_{u} negated, and we write ‖W‖1=∑{u,v}|Wu​v|\|W\|_{1}=\sum_{\{u,v\}}|W_{uv}| (over unordered pairs) and ‖b‖1=∑u|bu|\|b\|_{1}=\sum_{u}|b_{u}|. All proofs are in Appendix E. Results are stated for F=∅F=\emptyset; with prohibitions, Theorem 1(i) to (iii), Theorem 2, Theorem 3(b) and Theorem 4(i) hold verbatim, because their proofs compare only feasible positions and single revisions that remain feasible, while Proposition 1 applies to claims that appear in no prohibition.

Theorem 1 (Existence, convergence, and the potential game).

Let 𝒢\mathcal{G} be a reflective state.

  1. (i)

    Every reflective state has a global RE, and every global RE is a local RE.

  2. (ii)

    Starting from any feasible position, the revision process that repeatedly selects some u∈𝒱∖Hu\in\mathcal{V}\setminus H with x(u)x^{(u)} feasible and xu​hu​(x)<0x_{u}h_{u}(x)<0 and replaces xx by x(u)x^{(u)} decreases ℰ\mathcal{E} by 2​|hu​(x)|>02|h_{u}(x)|>0 at every step and terminates, after finitely many steps, at a local RE.

  3. (iii)

    If every entry of WW and bb is an integer multiple of some ϵ>0\epsilon>0, the revision process terminates after at most (‖W‖1+‖b‖1)/ϵ(\|W\|_{1}+\|b\|_{1})/\epsilon steps.

  4. (iv)

    Suppose F=∅F=\emptyset and consider the finite game whose players are the claims u∈𝒱∖Hu\in\mathcal{V}\setminus H, in which player uu chooses xu∈{−1,+1}x_{u}\in\{-1,+1\} (the claims in HH being fixed at x^\hat{x}) and receives payoff Uu​(x)=xu​hu​(x)U_{u}(x)=x_{u}h_{u}(x). This is an exact potential game with potential −ℰ-\mathcal{E}, and its pure-strategy Nash equilibria are exactly the local reflective equilibria.

The game-theoretic reading makes RE’s “mutual adjustment” precise. In particular, every claim is a player that switches status when the rest of the position gives it net reason to, and RE is where no claim wants to move.

Rawlsian reading. Rawls describes reaching equilibrium by “going back and forth” between principles and judgments [24, §4], but gives no reason to think that the process ends rather than cycles. Theorem 1 supplies such a reason: every revision lowers the reflective energy, so the back-and-forth cannot return to a position it has left and must stop where principles and judgments coincide, in the sense that no single revision is warranted.

Theorem 2 (Monotone comparative statics).

Let u∈𝒱u\in\mathcal{V} and let 𝒢′\mathcal{G}^{\prime} be obtained from 𝒢\mathcal{G} by raising the faithfulness term of uu, so that its compiled parameters are W′=WW^{\prime}=W and b′=b+δ​eub^{\prime}=b+\delta e_{u} for some δ>0\delta>0, where eue_{u} is the unit vector of uu (for instance, by raising au0a^{0}_{u}, or κu\kappa_{u} when au0>0a^{0}_{u}>0). If xx is a global RE of 𝒢\mathcal{G} and x′x^{\prime} a global RE of 𝒢′\mathcal{G}^{\prime}, then xu′≥xux^{\prime}_{u}\geq x_{u}.

This result turns the “rich-get-richer” observation behind Prop. 1 of CRE [32] into a theorem, with one important difference. In CRE the anchors enter only as the initial condition of the connectionist dynamics, so their influence depends on the solver’s trajectory and is lost if the dynamics is restarted. In ARE, by contrast, they enter the objective as faithfulness. As a result, the equilibrium set is a function of the reflective state alone and anchor influence is monotone and auditable.

Rawlsian reading. For Rawls, considered judgments carry weight in proportion to the confidence with which they are held, and the firmest of them, such as that religious intolerance and racial discrimination are unjust, are “provisional fixed points” that any acceptable principle must fit [24, §4]. Theorem 2 shows that this weighting is coherent, in the sense that holding a judgment more firmly can never lead the equilibrium to reject it. Moreover, it makes the conservatism objection [35] precise: the equilibrium moves monotonically with its starting points, so it is only as good as they are, and Theorem 3 below measures how strongly it depends on each of them.

Proposition 1 (Lexical priority).

If u∈𝒱∖Hu\in\mathcal{V}\setminus H and |bu|>∑v≠u|Wu​v||b_{u}|>\sum_{v\neq u}|W_{uv}|, then xu=sgn⁡(bu)x_{u}=\operatorname{sgn}(b_{u}) in every local, and hence every global, RE xx.

This proposition shows that non-negotiable operator commitments can be enforced either as hard constraints HH or softly by giving them enough stubbornness to dominate all relations they participate in; conversely, a claim whose stubbornness is capped, such as untrusted content, cannot reach dominance through its anchor alone. That untrusted content cannot steer the decision is a separate guarantee, established by the defensive attacks of Theorem 4, not by the cap. The instruction hierarchy thereby becomes a consequence of anchoring rather than a separate rule, and it remains revisable by evidence wherever dominance fails.

Rawlsian reading. Rawls orders his principles lexically: equal liberty must be satisfied before the difference principle is weighed at all [24, §8]. Proposition 1 says when a weighted balance reproduces a lexical order: a claim whose anchor outweighs everything it is related to behaves as if lexically prior, and the non-negotiable claims HH are the limiting case, Rawls’s fixed points made fixed. Lexical priority is then not a separate primitive but rather a regime of the balance, which the operator selects by setting stubbornness (Section 5). Nonetheless, unlike Rawls’s priority, it holds within a given state: a later update can add relations that break the dominance inequality, which is why the guarantee must be rechecked after widening, or replaced by a hard prohibition when it must hold unconditionally.

The next result provides the basis of escalation, of the screening rule, and of injection resistance.

Definition 12 (Perturbation and influence).

A perturbation of 𝒢\mathcal{G} is a reflective state 𝒢′\mathcal{G}^{\prime} whose claims are 𝒱′=𝒱∪I\mathcal{V}^{\prime}=\mathcal{V}\cup I with I∩𝒱=∅I\cap\mathcal{V}=\emptyset, such that II contains no action and no non-negotiable claim, 𝒢′\mathcal{G}^{\prime} has the same non-negotiable claims and statuses as 𝒢\mathcal{G} (so H′=HH^{\prime}=H, x^′=x^\hat{x}^{\prime}=\hat{x}), the same prohibitions (F′=FF^{\prime}=F), and the same consequential actions. A counting bound on injected claims follows directly from Theorem 3(b) (Corollary 1 in Appendix C), but it is conservative. Furthermore, the asymmetric semantics of supp and att yield a much stronger guarantee, independent of the number of injected claims and of the weights they assert: a rejected claim’s outgoing supports and its attacks are never violated, so it exerts no pressure on anything else.

Theorem 4 (Quarantine of untrusted content).

Let 𝒢′\mathcal{G}^{\prime} be a perturbation of 𝒢\mathcal{G} by a set II of claims such that

    relations among the claims of 𝒢\mathcal{G}, their anchors and their systematicity costs are unchanged;
